chkBrandEngineDecideWhich.message: An engine has to decide which entity this site IS before it can attribute an answer to you. It reconciles the names a page declares; with only one declaration there is nothing to reconcile, and with none there is nothing to attribute.

chkBrandTwoNamesOne.message: Two names for one site split it into two entities in the systems AI engines ground on, so half the evidence for citing you attaches to a name nobody asked about.

chkSameAsSameAsFieldKnowledge.message: sameAs is the field a knowledge graph follows to bind a site to an already-known entity (Wikipedia, Wikidata, LinkedIn, GitHub). It is the most direct machine-readable claim about identity a page can make, and it is the one AI grounding actually resolves.

chkSameAsSameAsFieldKnowledge2.message: sameAs is the field a knowledge graph follows to bind a site to an already-known entity (Wikipedia, Wikidata, LinkedIn, GitHub). Without it an engine has your name but no way to confirm you are the thing it already knows about.

chkAuthorDatePagesArticlesEngine.message: On pages that ARE articles, an engine weighing two candidate sources prefers the one it can attribute to someone and place in time.

chkAuthorDateEngineWeighingTwo.message: An engine weighing two candidate sources prefers the one it can attribute to someone and place in time. Unattributed, undated text is the easiest thing for it to pass over.

chkFreshAnythingUserCould.message: For anything a user could ask about "now", engines prefer a source they can date. An undated page is not judged stale — it is simply harder to justify citing.

chkFreshAnythingUserCould2.message: For anything a user could ask about "now", engines prefer a source they can date and that dates recently. A years-old declared date is a reason to reach for someone else.

chkHttpsInsecurePagesDemoted.message: Insecure pages are demoted or dropped by the crawlers that build the indexes AI answers are grounded on, and a browser blocking mixed content can leave a crawler reading a page the user never sees.

chkUrlShapeWhenAiAnswer.message: When an AI answer cites you it shows this string to the reader. A URL that states its own subject is the difference between a citation someone clicks and one they skim past.

chkStandingThesePagesReader.message: These are the pages a reader checks to decide whether a site is a real operation, and the same absence reads the same way to a model weighing whether to put your name behind an answer.

chkQHeadHeadingPhrasedQuestion.message: A heading phrased as the question a user would ask is the passage a retrieval system lifts. We can only detect that in languages our test covers.

chkQHeadHeadingPhrasedQuestion2.message: A heading phrased as the question a user would ask is the passage a retrieval system lifts out and attributes.

chkQHeadAIAnswersAssembled.message: AI answers are assembled from passages that already answer a question. A subheading written as the question makes the passage under it liftable as-is; one written as a label makes a model reconstruct what it was for.

chkStructListTableAlready.message: A list or a table is already the shape an answer is given in, so it can be lifted whole. The same facts in a paragraph have to be taken apart and reassembled first, and models reassemble badly.

chkSsrEngineDoesRun.message: An engine that does not run JavaScript sees only what the server sent. Measuring that means asking the server again, and this time we could not.

chkSsrReadPageS.message: Read from this page’s own address a second time, without running its JavaScript. Every variable except that one is held still — same origin, same browser, same moment — so a gap here is the page building itself in front of you and nowhere else. It carries your User-Agent, not a crawler’s, so a site that renders differently for bots is not being tested.
